title: What an agent session is

story: Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, finishes a run at 10:47 and the dashboard turns green. You open Jira to look at the plan, and there is nothing there. No plan, no Slack message, no branch. The harness, the small program that runs Nova inside the virtual machine (VM), wrote "success" into its status file because the last message from Nova's session said success.

It did say that. The same message also said is_error: true, and its text was an error from the API. Nobody had told the harness that "success" only means the turn ended normally, not that the work happened. Before you can trust an agent with a ticket, you have to know what it actually is and how to read what it reports.
hook.question: What is an agent session, and how do I read the messages it sends back without fooling myself?

read.h: One function call starts a whole program
p: The Claude Agent SDK is an npm package, @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk, and its main function is query(). You give it a prompt and an options object. It looks a bit like fetch(), but it does something much bigger: it starts Claude Code, the same program you use in your terminal, as a child process on your machine. The SDK even ships its own copy of the claude binary inside node_modules, so nothing else needs to be installed.

That program is the agent. It sends your prompt to the model, and when the model asks for a tool (read a file, run a command), the program runs the tool itself and sends the result back. One such round trip is a turn. The whole conversation, from your prompt to the final answer, with every turn in between, is a session. query() returns an async iterator: an object you read with for await, which hands you one message at a time as the session works.

Our first session is as small as it can be. It removes every built-in tool and loads no settings file, so the model can only answer with text. That leaves three parts to look at: the prompt, the model and the messages.

notes.text: query() returns at once. The claude process starts when you begin reading messages.
A full model ID, the cheapest model. Lesson p8-8 is about choosing models on purpose.
Effort is how much the model thinks before it answers: low, medium, high, xhigh or max.
An empty list removes Read, Bash, Edit and the rest. The next lesson gives tools back on purpose.
Load no settings files: not ~/.claude/settings.json, not .claude/ in the folder, not CLAUDE.md.

read.h: Read the messages one by one
p: Every message has a type field, and TypeScript narrows the message when you test it, so inside each branch you only see the fields that exist. A session always starts with a system message whose subtype is init: it says which model, which binary version and which tools this session really has. Then come assistant messages, each carrying one content block (a piece of text, a tool call, or thinking), and user messages, which carry tool results back to the model. The last message of a turn is the result.

Look at the last line of the loop. The final text lives in msg.result, but only on a result whose subtype is "success". If you read msg.result without that check, the TypeScript compiler refuses, because the error results have no such field. The lab shows you that error, and it is a friendly one: the types are telling you that a session can end in more than one way.

notes.text: for await reads one message at a time. The loop ends when the session ends.
init is always first. Its tools list is the truth about what this session can use.
assistant and user messages wrap the API message, so the blocks are at msg.message.content.
Keep the session ID: you need it to continue this conversation later (lesson p8-6).
result exists only on a success. Remove the check and the compiler stops you.

read.h: The result message is the receipt
p: The harness keeps very little from a session, and almost all of it comes from the result message. Three questions matter. Did it work? Read subtype and is_error together. The subtype says how the turn ended: "success", or an error subtype such as error_max_turns or error_during_execution. is_error says whether it ended on an error, and that is the trap from the story: when the API itself fails, the turn can end with subtype "success", is_error true, and the error text in result. What did it cost? modelUsage is a map from model ID to tokens and an estimated price, and it counts everything the session called, including helper agents. The older usage field counts only the main loop. Which session was it? session_id names the transcript, so you can continue it later.

Two more details save you from bugs. total_cost_usd and modelUsage are estimates from the SDK, not a bill. In our platform the real numbers come from the gateway, our service that adds the API key to every model call and counts what it costs. And when a single-prompt session ends on an error result, query() yields that result and then throws, so wrap the loop in try and catch if your code must continue.

notes.text: modelUsage covers every model the session used, helpers included. costUSD is an estimate.
An error subtype: the session stopped early, for example at a limit.
The trap: subtype success, but the turn ended on an API error. The error text is in result.

deeper.h: Go deeper: which claude runs, and the /core entry
p: By default the SDK starts the binary it shipped with; in the lab that is Claude Code 2.1.301. Your terminal's claude may be a different version, and versions differ in small ways. The option pathToClaudeCodeExecutable points the SDK at one exact binary instead. Our harness uses it so every VM runs the same binary that passed the nightly smoke test.

Programs that bundle all their code into one file import from @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk/core instead of the root. It exports the same query(), tool() and createSdkMcpServer(), but takes zod and the MCP library from your own install instead of carrying its own copies. Never import both the root and /core in one process: they are separate bundles, and you would load two copies of the SDK's state.

lab.title: Start a session and read its receipt
needs: For the last steps only: your own Anthropic API key from platform.claude.com (a few cents of credit is plenty)
lab.goal: Install the Agent SDK, let the compiler teach you the shapes of a session's messages, then run one session with your own key and report its result honestly.

guess.q: Your script checks only msg.subtype === "success". The API rejects the request because your key has expired. What does your script print?

options.text: Nothing: the session crashes before any message arrives.
options.why: The claude process still sends a result message that describes what happened. A crash with no result is rarer, for example when the process cannot start at all.
An API error can end the turn with subtype "success" and is_error true, with the error text in result. Checking only subtype calls that a success.

options.text: error_during_execution, because every failure has its own subtype.
options.why: Error subtypes are for turns that stopped early, like hitting a limit. An API error at the end of a turn is reported through is_error.

follow.say: Make a scratch project. The SDK runs real sessions, so keep it away from fcp. tsx runs TypeScript files directly, and typescript gives you the compiler.
follow.do:
mkdir ~/sdk-lab && cd ~/sdk-lab && npm init -y && npm pkg set type=module
npm install @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk zod
npm install -D tsx typescript @types/node
follow.see:
added 105 packages, and audited 106 packages in 6s
…
added 7 packages, and audited 113 packages in 3s
found 0 vulnerabilities

follow.say: Look inside node_modules. The SDK brought its own claude binary as a second package for your platform; on an Apple Silicon Mac it is called darwin-arm64.
Ask the types how a session can end. This line lists every error subtype a result can have.
Add a tsconfig.json with strict mode, then write src/session.ts from the Understand step, but with the last line as console.log("said", msg.result), without the success check. Run the compiler.
follow.do:
cat > tsconfig.json <<'EOF'
{ "compilerOptions": { "target": "es2023", "module": "nodenext", "strict": true, "noEmit": true, "skipLibCheck": true }, "include": ["src", "test"] }
EOF
npx tsc
follow.see:
src/session.ts(22,29): error TS2339: Property 'result' does not exist on type 'SDKResultMessage'.
  Property 'result' does not exist on type 'SDKResultError'.

follow.say: Put the success check back, so the final text is read only where it exists. The compiler now has nothing to say.
follow.do:
# last line: if (msg.subtype === "success") console.log("said", msg.result);
npx tsc && echo clean

follow.say: Now run the session for real. This is the one step that needs your own API key; it costs far less than a cent on Haiku.
follow.do:
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...   # your own key
npx tsx src/session.ts
follow.see: (Needs your key, so here is what to look for rather than exact output.) An init line with claude-haiku-5-5 and 2.1.301, an assistant line with one text block saying pong, a result line with success and is_error false, a tiny cost, the model list, a session ID, and said pong.

follow.say: Run it a second time and compare the session lines. Every query() call is a new session unless you ask to continue an old one.
follow.see: (Needs your key.) A different session ID from the first run.

lab.build: Write src/report.ts from the Understand step and change the result branch of src/session.ts to print report(msg). Wrap the loop in try and catch, because a single-prompt session throws after an error result. Then run it twice with your key: once normally, where report prints an OK line, and once with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=not-a-real-key in front of the command, where report must print FAILED or STOPPED and your catch must keep the script from crashing.
checks: The bundled binary prints a version when you call it with --version.
npx tsc reports TS2339 when you read msg.result without the success check, and nothing once the check is back.
With your key, two runs print two different session IDs.
With a wrong key, report prints FAILED or STOPPED, never OK, and the script ends without a stack trace.
lab.fix: A teammate's status page shows every agent run in green. Their code is if (msg.type === "result" && msg.subtype === "success") markGreen(). Yesterday the gateway was down for ten minutes and every run in that window is green too. Find the field they forgot, and change the condition so an API error turns the run red.
explain: What does query() start on your machine, and why does that mean the agent can run tools without any code of yours?
A result has subtype "success". What else must you check before you call the run a success, and why?
Why is modelUsage the field to add up for cost, and not usage?
lab.done: You can run a session, point at the init, assistant and result messages in its output, and your report never calls a failed run OK.

check.q: Nova used two helper agents during a run. Where do you read what the whole run cost?

options.text: Add up total_cost_usd from every result message the session sent
options.why: In a long session each result carries the running total so far, so adding them counts the same money several times.

options.text: modelUsage on the last result message
options.why: modelUsage lists every model the session called, helpers included, and the last result has the latest totals.

options.text: The usage field on the result message
options.why: usage counts only the main loop. The helpers' calls are missing from it.

check.q: A result message has subtype "success". Can the harness mark the run as done?

options.text: Yes, success means the model finished its answer
options.why: When the turn ends on an API error, subtype can still be success. The error text is then in result.
num_turns counts round trips with the model. It says nothing about errors.

options.text: Only if is_error is also false
options.why: subtype says how the turn ended; is_error says whether it ended on an error. You need both.

check.q: What does query() actually do when you start reading its messages?

options.text: It starts the claude program as a child process, which talks to the model and runs the tools itself
options.why: That is why the agent can read files and run commands without any tool code of yours: the claude process does it.

options.text: It sends one HTTP request to the API and streams back the answer
options.why: That is the plain client SDK. query() runs a whole agent loop with many requests and tool calls.

options.text: It starts an agent on Anthropic's servers, which runs tools in the cloud
options.why: The process runs on your machine, in your folder. Only the model calls go over the network.

p: Inside every VM, nova-worker is one query() call with a long options object: the model and effort from the routing table, the fcp checkout as its working folder, our tools and hooks, and the gateway instead of an API key. It writes the session ID, the subtype and is_error into its status file, so the workflow knows whether a step worked and which session to continue after a question to a person.

Smaller sessions follow the same shape. The readiness check, which decides whether a ticket is clear enough to start, is one cheap session with no tools that reads only the result. And the harness always points pathToClaudeCodeExecutable at the binary baked into the VM image, so every run uses the same tested Claude Code.

tickets.why: nova-worker is a query() session; it reads the result message the way this lesson does.
The readiness check is a no-tools session whose verdict comes from the result.
The workflow spike checks that modelUsage counts every agent of a run.
Bakes the pinned claude binary that pathToClaudeCodeExecutable points to.

words.plain: One conversation with the agent: your prompt, every turn and tool call, and the final result. It has an ID.
The SDK function that starts a session and returns its messages one at a time.
One round trip inside the session: the model answers, maybe asks for tools, and the tool results go back.
The last message of a turn: subtype, is_error, cost, modelUsage and the session ID.
Tokens and estimated cost per model for everything the session called, helper agents included.

review.q: Write the three if-branches of a message loop from memory: which types, and which field you print in each.
review.a: system with subtype init (model, version, tools), assistant (msg.message.content), result (subtype, is_error, modelUsage, session_id, and result only on success).

review.q: Your report says OK but nothing happened. Name the first two fields you look at.
review.a: is_error, because an API error can end a turn with subtype success, and result, which then holds the error text.

remember: A session is one query() call that runs Claude Code for you; trust the result only when subtype is success and is_error is false.
